## 8. Sentences of the specification made false, which this rung's section does not name

Each states the order of attempts without the numeral's exception. The gather corrects them.

- `Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:526-529`: "For a given functional call, we first determine whether there exists a declaration that is applicable without coercion. If so, the most specific declaration is selected".
- `Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:544-547`, the callout `revival-overloading`: "a coercion makes a call possible and never changes which declaration runs when one is applicable without it".
- `Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:606-608`: "If Σ is not empty then we use the overloading resolution described in ... to determine which element of Σ is called."
- `Specification/basic/inference.tex:60-61`: "So a coercion is applied only to make a call possible: it never changes which declaration is chosen when one is applicable to the call without it."
- `Specification/basic/inference.tex:334-336`: "in the choice among declarations that are applicable to the call only with coercion and that the numeral would otherwise leave tied": the tie rule now holds also where the tied declarations differ at another argument (fork N2).
- `Specification/appendices/changes.tex:2124-2125` and `:2898-2899`, the Rationales of `revival-inference` and `revival-overloading`, which state the decision of 28 September 2026 with no word of the numeral's exception.
- `Specification/appendices/changes.tex:3801-3804`, the Effect of `revival-numeral-type`: "A numeral beside a value of an integer type is converted to that type where no declaration of the operator is applicable to the two without coercion".

Outside the specification: FACTS F-346 and the last sentence of F-349; the skill's `references/revival-changes.md`, "Under walk it is `false` (row 973)" (`record.md`).

====F
## Sentences that the change makes false

None in `Specification/`: `grep -rniE "generic function.*(value|argument)|polymorphic function.*(value|passed)" Specification/appendices Specification/basic/functions.tex Specification/basic/inference.tex` prints nothing, and no Effect of Appendix I names row 156 (the section's own grep). In the record, row 758's notes say that walk refuses `useOne(count)` "as row 156 gives"; walk now runs it (`GenericFunctionAsValueWalk` asserts 1). Row 758 is rung C's to close.

===B
## Sentences of the specification made false

None. `Specification/basic/variables.tex:15-16` and `Specification/basic/expressions/aggregate.tex:15`, "matrix unpasting ... not yet supported", stay true. No Effect of `Specification/appendices/changes.tex` and no note names a top-level array literal.

===C
## 8. The specification

Changed, each before and after:

- `Specification/basic/expressions/reductions.tex:30-31`, in the box `revival-reductions`. Before: "Neither implementation directs it by the type N of the expression yet." After: "Neither implementation desugars a reduction by the type N of the expression yet: each instantiates the big operator that the reduction names."
- `reductions.tex:44-79`. Before: "takes the bound of the big operator's static parameter, which is not the element type, or, where the reduction's type at that bound does not fit the reduction's expected type, that expected type ...: a bound such as Number gives the reduction that type where it has no expected type, and a bound that mentions the static parameter itself gives no instance that applies, so that the reduction is refused (row 425). Until the compiled type checker directs the desugaring by type, a reduction with a generator clause list whose element type no argument fixes writes its static argument in a program that both implementations are to run, as the team's own tests do, as in ...". After: the bound where the reduction so instantiated is accepted and fits; otherwise the expected type, then the body's type; where the two implementations instantiate alike and where they differ (rows 1008, 1007); the argument is written where they would differ.
- `Specification/basic/inference.tex:224-260`: a new paragraph, "A reference to a generic function", with its box.
- `inference.tex:437-447` (a sentence the section does not name, in the same file). Before: "and it refuses the reduction where the big operator has no instance at its bound, as one whose bound mentions its own static parameter has none (row 425 of the revival's gap ledger)." 427	## Revival changes, for the skill writer
428	
429	One subsection for each landed rung: its "Revival change" section as its record gave it, both parts word for word, with each placeholder replaced by its row's number and its own headings one level lower. The lines cited are those of the rung's branch.
430	
431	### Rung P, `rung-parser-declarations`: two forms that the parser refused
432	
433	**The change.**
434	
435	- The team's parser reads U+2211 and U+220F as operator characters: `singleOp` takes any character that the operator table knows (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/parser/Symbol.rats:175-178` at `db352c1776`; `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/parser_util/precedence_resolver/Operators.java:2080-2082`), and only the words `SUM` and `PROD` begin a reduction (`Symbol.rats:252-254` at `db352c1776`). So `∑[i <- 1#3] i` was a `Syntax Error`, and `∑ x` a call of a prefix operator named `SUM`. The tree now reads each sign exactly as its word: it begins a reduction and, after `opr`, declares `BIG +` or `BIG juxtaposition`; as an infix or postfix operator, or in an import's list, it is a `Syntax Error`. Tests: `ProjectFortress/tests/SumSignAccumulator.fss`, `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/SumSignAccumulatorCompiled.test`. The reason: the specification's grammar, `Accumulator ::= ∑ | ∏ | BIG (Encloser | Op)` (`Specification/basic/expressions/reductions.tex:20`), and its operator header, which takes `∑` and `∏` (`Specification/appendices/grammars/concrete-syntax.tex:739-740`).
436	- The team's parser refuses, in an api, a postfix operator whose sign is an exponent operator, as `opr (x: ZZ32)^T: ZZ32`: `Syntax Error` at column 1 of the next line (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/parser/Parameter.rats:171-172` at `db352c1776`, which lacks the `/` of `:141-142`). The tree now takes in an api what it takes in a component. Tests: `ProjectFortress/tests/ApiPostfixExponentOp.fss`, `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/ApiPostfixExponentOpCompiled.test`. The reason: the specification's grammar gives the api's header the same three alternatives as the component's (`Specification/appendices/grammars/concrete-syntax.tex:726-727`, `:737-738`).
437	
438	**Provenance.** Gap ledger rows 133 and 5; fork P1 of climb batch 32's record, `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-32.md`, "Forks the batch takes", taken at its default; P-87, under which no model line changes; climb batch 32, rung P.
439	
440	### Rung S, `rung-superscript-after`: a superscript after a dotted access and after a parenthesised call
441	
442	#### The change
443	
444	The team's parser gave a primary with a dot no place for a superscript: `PrimaryItem` chose between `LeftAssociatedPrimary`, which took subscripts, parenthesised items and selectors, and `MathPrimary`, the only production with math items (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/parser/Expression.rats:384-386` and `:463-474` at `a874948ac`), so `p.wq^T`, `B.n^2` and `B.f()^T` were a bare `Syntax Error` under walk and compiled. The team's walk refused a postfix operator after any tight juxtaposition that is a call or after any exponentiation, also where it stood in parentheses: `(f(x))^T`, `(f(x))!` and `(a^b)!` stopped with "Syntax Error: a function argument should not be immediately followed by a non-expression element." or "an exponentiation should not be immediately followed by a non-expression element." (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java`, `forOpExpr`), where the team's checker accepted them.
445	
446	The tree now reads a primary with a dot as the front of the math items that follow it: `p.wq^T` is `(p.wq)^T`, `a.m(x)^T` is `(a.m(x))^T`, `p.wq^T x` is the juxtaposition of `(p.wq)^T` and `x`, and `B.n^2^2` is the static error of two exponentiations. A subscript, a parenthesised item or a tight identifier after a dotted method call parses in the same way (`B.f()[5]`). Walk evaluates a parenthesised operand of a postfix operator as one expression, so `(f(x))^T` has the value that the compiled path gives. `f(x)^T`, a call followed directly by a superscript, is still a static error on both paths. Tests: `ProjectFortress/tests/SuperscriptAfterDottedAccess.fss`, `ProjectFortress/tests/SuperscriptAfterParenthesisedCall.fss`, `ProjectFortress/tests/SuperscriptAfterCallRefused.fss`, and their compiled forms in `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/`.
447	
448	The reason: the specification. "A tight juxtaposition is always left-associated if it contains any dot" (`Specification/basic/operators/juxtameaning.tex:130-131`); its grammar gives `Primary ^ Exponent` and `Primary ExponentOp` where `Primary.Id` and a parenthesised expression are each a `Primary` (`Specification/appendices/grammars/concrete-syntax.tex:937-953`, `Specification/basic/expressions/operator-app.tex:29-32`); and its static error is for an argument "immediately followed by a non-expression element" (`juxtameaning.tex:156-162`), which a parenthesised call is not. Measured on the code before the change: `x.v^T` gives `Syntax Error` at the `^` on both paths, and `(f(3))^T` gives walk's refusal and 104 compiled.
449	
450	Still so: a selector after a superscript, `B.data^T.v`, is a syntax error; write `(B.data^T).v`. A subscript followed by a superscript where the subscript is a math item, `x[5]^2` or `B.f()[5]^2`, fails on both paths; write `(x[5])^2`. `B.data[5]^2`, whose subscript belongs to the dotted primary, runs.

456	### Rung C, `rung-static-argument-inferred`: two static arguments that the compiled checker left open
457	
458	#### The change
459	
460	The team's sources and what they say or do:
461	
462	- The specification directs a reduction's desugaring by the type of its expression, "a sum is desugared with the reduction for the type N of the expression" (`Specification/basic/expressions/reductions.tex:28`), and says of a reference to a polymorphic function that "the static arguments are statically inferred from the context of the function call" (`Specification/basic/expressions/var-ref.tex:38-39`). It gives no rule for either inference.
463	- The team's checker typed the big operator's call alone, as an argument of `__bigOperator`, and refused a reduction with generators whose big operator's bound names its own static parameter, as `SUM[j <- 0#i] f(j)`: "Could not check call to operator BIG + ... is not applicable to an argument of type ()." It gave a generic function passed as a value the function's own type with its static parameters, and stopped with an internal error, 'F is not in the kind env [][][]', where that type met a parameter type.
464	
465	What the tree now does:
466	
467	- A reduction with generators that writes no static argument is accepted by the compiled checker. Where the call is accepted with the big operator instantiated alone (a plain bound), nothing changes. Otherwise the big operator is instantiated by the reduction's expected type, where the type meets the big operator's bound, the reduction so instantiated is accepted and its type converts to the expected type; the elements are converted to it. Otherwise it is instantiated by the type of the reduction's body, a numeral at its default. So `x: RR64 = SUM[j <- 0#n] f(j)` with `f` answering `ZZ32` sums in `RR64`, and `t = SUM[j <- 0#n] f(j)` in `ZZ32`. A reduction written as a call's argument takes its body's type where the call is accepted so. A big operator with two or more static parameters, as `BIG MIN_MAX`, still needs them written for the checker. 478	### Rung N, `rung-numeral-most-specific`: a numeral at a call goes to the most specific declaration
479	
480	**The change.**
481	
482	- The team's source: the specification's coercion chapter chooses a declaration applicable without coercion before any that a coercion reaches ("we first determine whether there exists a declaration that is applicable without coercion. If so, the most specific declaration is selected", `Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:526-528`), and the revival's own text read a numeral so until this change: a numeral was applicable without coercion to a parameter of its default type and to one that fixes no type, and "its conversion into any other type is a coercion" (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:111-114` at db352c1776). The interpreter's library declares `opr =(a:Any, b:Any)` and `opr =/=(a:Any, b:Any)` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:96-98`), which a numeral fits at its default.
483	- What the tree does now: at a call, a numeral goes to the most specific declaration that takes it, by its own coercion if need be. Where one declaration fits the numeral at its default and another is reached only by the numeral's own coercion, every other argument fitting as it is, the second runs when its declared parameter types lie strictly below the first's by subtyping. So `u = 0` and `0 = u` are `true` and `u =/= 0` is `false` for a zero `u` of `NN32`, `NN64` or `RR32`, on both paths; `h = 0.5` is `true` for `h: QQ = 1/2`; `k(5)` runs `k(x: NN32)` beside `k(x: Any)`; `case u of 0 => ...` matches a zero `NN32`; a program's own number type with a numeral coercion and its own `=` compares with a numeral by that `=`. Where the two declarations are not ordered by subtyping, the one that the numeral's default fits runs: `f(1.5)` beside `f(x: RR32)` and `f(x: RR64)` runs the `RR64` declaration. Of two declarations that a call reaches only by coercion and that are not ordered, the one that the numeral's default fits runs, also where they differ at another argument: `mul(1.0, f)` for `f: RR32` runs `mul(a: RR64, b: RR64)` beside a program's `mul(a: Q, b: Q)`, and `1.0 s` for `s: ZZ32` is `RR64`'s juxtaposition. A value's coercion still never changes which declaration runs. `Equality[\T\]` declares `opr =/=(self, other:T)` as `NOT (self = other)`, so `=/=` reaches a type's own `=` for every type that extends `Equality`. A value whose static type is `Any` or `Number` fixes no type for a numeral beside it, which takes its default: the compiled checker answers so, and walk, which has no static types, reads the value's run-time type, so for `a: Any` holding a zero `NN32` walk answers `a = 0` `true`. Tests: `compiler_tests/NumeralMostSpecificCompiled`, `compiler_tests/NumeralTieDefaultCompiled`, `tests/NumeralMostSpecificWalk`, `tests/NumeralEqualsNumberWalk`, `tests/NotEqualNumeral`; the expected failure `tests/XXXNumeralBesideAnyWalk` for walk's departure.
484	- The reason, as evidence: with no `=` between a numeral type and a number type, `u = 0` met the library's `=` over `(Any, Any)`, which the numeral's default `ZZ32` fits, and `SEQV` of an `NN32` and a `ZZ32` is `false`: walk printed 'FAIL: u = 0 for an NN32 zero' on the code before the change. On the compiled path `k(5)` beside `k(x: Any)` and `k(x: NN32)` died with 'NoSuchMethodError ... \=k{...}(fortress.AnyType$Any)', and the checker refused `mul(1.0, f)`: 'Ambiguous coercion in call to function mul'. The Working Draft says that `e =/= e'` is `NOT (e = e')` (`Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:272`).
485	
486	**Provenance.**
487	
488	- The question: rows 973 and 966 of the gap ledger, the static numerals probe's question 1, and the review of the ways to `true` (`explorations/reviews/numeral-equality-ways-2026-11-10.md`, way B).

492	### Rung F, `rung-generic-function-value`: a generic function passed as a value under walk
493	
494	**The change.** The team's walk gave a function with static parameters no type as a value: `Fcn.type()` returned null for it, and the team's comment there says "FGenericFunction never calls setFtype and this returns null in that case. This leads to extensive bugs particularly when a generic function is overloaded along with non-generic siblings, or when a generic function is passed as an argument to an overloaded function without providing an explicit type instantiation" (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/Fcn.java:58-66` at `db352c1776`). So `app(half, v)`, for `half[\nat n\](x: Vector[\RR64,n\]): Vector[\RR64,n\]` and `app(f: Vector[\RR64,3\] -> Vector[\RR64,3\], v: Vector[\RR64,3\])`, stopped with 'Unification error: ... got arg half[\nat n\](...) ... of type null', and only `app(half[\3\], v)` ran. The tree now runs `app(half, v)`: the parameter receives `half` at 3, the instance that a direct call with a `Vector[\RR64,3\]` runs. A parameter of a function or a constructor, a local variable declared with an arrow type and a variable of arrow type at an assignment receive so. A generic callee's static parameters are fixed by its other arguments first, so `rows(half, m)` runs for `rows[\nat r, nat c\](f: Vector[\RR64,c\] -> Vector[\RR64,c\], m: Matrix[\RR64,r,c\])`. Where the receiving type leaves a static parameter of the function open, and at `Any`, a type parameter or an untyped variable, the value stays generic, and each application infers its static arguments from its arguments' run-time types. An overloaded name with a generic declaration stays the whole overloaded function at an arrow-typed place. Two cases still depart: an immutable top-level variable of arrow type keeps the generic value, so a call at another size runs; and a generic function passed at `f: T -> T` where a value fixes the callee's `T` by its run-time type is refused; write the static argument there, `appT(half[\3\], v)`. Tests: `ProjectFortress/tests/GenericFunctionAsValueWalk.fss`, `GenericFunctionRowLiftWalk.fss`, `GenericFunctionAssignedWalk.fss`; the two departures, `XXXGenericFunctionTopLevelVariableWalk.fss` and `XXXGenericFunctionAtTypeParameterWalk.fss`. The reason: the specification makes a function a value and says of a reference to a polymorphic function that "most identifier references do not include them.; the static arguments are statically inferred from the context of the function call" (`Specification/basic/expressions/var-ref.tex:35-40`); walk has no static types, so the context it can read is the type of the place that receives the value, and the call.
495	
496	**Provenance.** The item: ledger row 156, and the model's four vector functions passed to the row lift (`explorations/reviews/c4-fortress-way-2026-11-15.md`, section 1.2). The default followed: fork F1 of `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-32.md`, "Forks the batch takes", within P-48 and P-12; P-87 keeps the model's lines. The batch: climb batch 32, rung F.

498	### Rung B, `rung-toplevel-array-literal`: an array literal at the top level under walk
499	
500	**The change.** The team's walk bound a top-level variable declared with an array type to the literal's paste, a tuple, and stopped: `shp: ZZ32[3] = [27 16 27]` gave 'Type mismatch binding (27,16,27): (ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32) (type (ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)) to shp (type Array1[\ZZ32,0,3\])'; only a declaration in a block built the array (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/LHSEvaluator.java:170-207`, the block's binding; `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/BuildEnvironments.java:788-803`, the top-level check, which built nothing). The tree now builds a top-level literal with a declared array type into the library array of that type, for an immutable and a `var` variable, with numerals, names, expressions, strings or pasted arrays as elements, and a field of an object declared so (`ProjectFortress/tests/ObjectFieldArrayLiteral.fss`); a reader above the declaration sees the array; a literal of another size than its declared type, or with an element that is not of the element type, is refused at load. Test: `ProjectFortress/tests/TopLevelArrayLiteral.fss`, with `TopLevelArrayLiteralSize` and `TopLevelArrayLiteralElement` for the refusals. The reason: the specification gives an array expression one type wherever it stands, `Arrayk[\T, 0, n0, ...\]` (`Specification/basic/expressions/aggregate.tex`, "Array Expressions"), and a top-level declaration `id : Type = expr` the same meaning as a local one (`Specification/basic/variables.tex`, "Top-Level Variable Declarations"). Still so: a top-level literal without a declared type is bound as its paste and fails at its first use; write the type. A literal in a block of another size than its declared type is not refused; a `var` bound to a literal in a block is immutable; a literal assigned to a variable is not built.
501	
502	**Provenance.** Ledger row 142; the batch's fork B1, "A typed array literal at the top level is the array that the same literal is in a function body", built within P-87 (no model line changes) and P-173 (a numeral element converts at the element type); climb batch 32, rung B.
503	
504	### Rung D, `rung-tuple-binding`: a top-level tuple binding on the compiled path
505	
506	**The change.** The team's code generator refuses a top-level declaration of several names: `forVarDeclPrePass` throws 'VarDecl … tupled lhs not handled.' where the left side has more than one name (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:6475-6477` at `db352c1776`), and the team's checker, in its case for a tuple expression of as many elements, rebuilds the right side without a type, so that each name has none (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Decls.scala:270-272` at `db352c1776`). The tree now compiles the form: each name is a top-level variable of its declared type or its element's type, a numeral element at its default, and the right side is evaluated once, when the first of its names is read (`ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/TopLevelTupleBindingCompiled.test`). A use of a name at another type is refused (`ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXTopLevelTupleBindingType.test`, whose prefix is the harness's mark of a compile that must fail). A name's declared type is checked against its element also where other names of the binding declare none and the right side is a call (`ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/TopLevelTupleBindingMixedTypes.test`, `XXXTopLevelTupleBindingMixedRefused.test`): the team's checker leaves such a name unchecked, as it still does in a local tuple binding (`ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXLocalTupleBindingMixedTypes.test`). The reason: the specification gives the form for every top-level declaration, "All forms can be used with tuple notation to declare multiple variables together" (`Specification/basic/variables.tex:99`), and a variable's value "is computed to be the value of the initializer expression" (`:63`); walk's own desugaring states the same design, "Introduce a temporary, then initialize elements piece-by-piece" (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/rewrite/DesugarerVisitor.java:858-859`). Walk departs from it: its right side runs once for each name and once more (`ProjectFortress/tests/XXXTopLevelTupleBindingOnceWalk.fss`).
507	
508	**Provenance.** The item: rows 988 and 474 of the gap ledger, and the model's hyperparameter lines, which P-9 keeps as tuple bindings. The default it follows: fork D1 of CLIMB-BATCH-32.md, "Each name of a tuple binding is a top-level variable of its element's type; the right side is evaluated once", and fork D2, the code generator's half for a top-level binding only; P-173 for a numeral element's default. The batch: climb batch 32, rung D.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The record's tool: it owns the form of FACTS.md and POSITIONS.md and of
their two history files, and is the only way to write them.

An entry is one line under a permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.` in
explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md and `- P-48 **Title.** Text.` in
POSITIONS.md. A number is never reused or changed: a new entry takes the
highest number its file has ever used, plus one. An entry stands under the
nearest `## ` or `### ` heading above it, its section. Its title is its bold
opening, or where it has none, its opening words up to the first colon,
semicolon or full stop.

A pointer is another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, alone
(`It builds P-48.`) or with the first words of the target's title in quotes
(`It builds P-48, "A type parameter the arguments do not fix ..."`, or
`P-48 ("...")`). Quoted words must open the target's current title (`...` or
`…` marks words left out); when an entry is retitled, the tool rewrites them
in every entry that points to it, in the same call.

The history (FACTS-history.md, POSITIONS-history.md beside the record) holds,
under `### F-87`, one block per change, oldest first: one provenance line (the
UTC time from the clock, the kind of change, `from` each report section,
`commit`, `by`, then the note after a colon), and the line as it stood before
the change. The tool derives the kind: `added`, `rewritten`, `moved to "S"`,
`merged into F-n`, `F-n merged in`, `removed`, `noted`; the numbering wrote one
`numbered` block per entry. A retitle that refreshed other entries' pointer
words, or a merge that moved their pointers, says so in one more line of the
block (`pointer words refreshed in: F-12, P-48`).

A `noted` block, which `note` writes, leaves the entry as it is. It adds what
the entry's history lacks, such as the curator's messages behind a text kept
word for word, with their times, or a correction of an earlier block. It holds
no earlier line, and its note says what it adds, so it needs one. A gone entry
takes none: its last block stays `merged into` or `removed`. A noted block
that corrects an earlier block names it by its time, in the field after the
kind: `correcting the block of 2026-10-13 19:07Z`, or, where blocks of the
entry share that minute, `correcting the 2nd block of 2026-10-14 04:41Z`,
counted oldest first. The block corrected is never edited.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .record.lock beside the record), checks the
